A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with numbered input nodes,
constant nodes, and gates from the fixed basis $\{\mathsf{AND},\mathsf{OR},\mathsf{NOT}\}$;
AND and OR gates have two predecessors, NOT gates have one, and constants
have values zero or one. Its output is one designated node. A family
$(C_n)_{n\ge0}$ has exactly $n$ input nodes labeled $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ in
$C_n$ and polynomially many nodes as a function of $n+2$. The family is
**logspace-uniform** when a deterministic read-only-input logspace transducer,
on input $1^n$ and a query with binary node indices of length $O(\log(n+2))$,
halts and answers the size, gate-type (including input labels and constant
values), and predecessor queries for the
topologically numbered encoding of $C_n$, and answers which numbered gate is
the designated output. In particular, it can stream that polynomial-length
encoding without storing it.

derivations.claim: Fix one valid query to the indexed transducer. Its read-only input and query tapes have polynomially many head positions in $n$, its work tapes use $O(\log(n+2))$ cells over a fixed alphabet, and its finite control has finitely many states. Thus it has at most $(n+2)^c$ internal configurations for some fixed $c$. A halting deterministic computation cannot repeat an internal configuration: because the input tapes are read-only and the output tape is write-only, a repetition would repeat the same future transitions forever. Hence each size, type, predecessor, or output query takes polynomial time and writes polynomially many bits.

Query the total node count $N_n\le n+q(n)$ once. For every index $1,\ldots,N_n$, query its type, recording its input label or constant value when applicable, and query every predecessor required by that type; also query the designated output. This includes all $n$ input nodes wherever they occur in the topological order. There are polynomially many queries, each of polynomial time by step 1.1. Every node index is at most $n+q(n)$, so each self-delimiting index has $O(\log(n+q(n)+2))$ bits. Writing the input-count header and all records therefore takes polynomial time and produces a polynomial-length full list.

Each record is the exact gate type, input label or constant value, and predecessor data returned for that same topological node, and the final output field is the exact designated node. The full-list decoder consequently evaluates the same ordered DAG on every input, including the case $n=0$ when the input list is empty.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, let $K$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite instrument** from $H$ to $K$ is a family of complex-linear maps $\mathcal I_a:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$, one for each $a\in\Omega$, such that each $\mathcal I_a$ is completely positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and

$$\sum_{a\in\Omega}\operatorname{tr}_K(\mathcal I_a(X))=\operatorname{tr}_H(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H).$$

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (nonnegative with trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), define the outcome weight $p_a(\rho):=\operatorname{tr}_K(\mathcal I_a(\rho))$. The **conditional state** for outcome $a$ is

$$\rho_a:=\begin{cases}\mathcal I_a(\rho)/p_a(\rho),&p_a(\rho)>0,\\[2pt]\bot,&p_a(\rho)=0.\end{cases}$$

Here $\bot$ is a symbol meaning that no conditional density operator is assigned; it is not a state. Positivity and normalization of the outcome weights, and density of every positive-probability conditional state, are proved in [[thm-qc-instrument-outcome-law-normalizes]] and [[thm-qc-instrument-conditional-state-is-density]].

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and write $\mathcal L(H)$ and $\mathcal L(K)$ for their vector spaces of complex-linear endomorphisms with pointwise operations ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]], [[prop-linear-maps-form-a-vector-space]]). Let $\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be complex-linear. For each integer $r\ge1$, put $R=\mathbb C^r$ with its standard ordered register basis ([[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]]). Write an operator $X\in\mathcal L(H\otimes R)$ in its unique $r\times r$ block form $X=[X_{ij}]$ with $X_{ij}\in\mathcal L(H)$, and define $\Phi^{(r)}(X)$ to have blocks $[\Phi(X_{ij})]$ on $K\otimes R$. Lemma [[lem-qc-finite-ancilla-amplification-is-block-map]] proves that this block rule defines a linear map on the full operator space for every finite $r$. For $r=1$, the extension is $\Phi$ under the canonical unitary identifications $x\mapsto x\otimes e_0$ and $y\mapsto y\otimes e_0$ proved in that lemma.

The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** if, for every finite $r\ge1$, $\Phi^{(r)}$ sends every nonnegative operator on $H\otimes R$ to a nonnegative operator on $K\otimes R$ ([[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]). The quantifier includes $r=1$; complete positivity therefore implies positivity. No Kraus, Choi, or Stinespring characterization is part of this definition.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces with specified ordered orthonormal bases of
sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the
factor bases, ordered lexicographically, form an orthonormal basis of the
tensor register, and

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

For the empty list the product is $1$ and the tensor space is $\mathbb C$; if
any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

derivations.claim: Each basis projection $P_a$ and $Q_b$ is diagonal with entries $0$ or $1$, hence self-adjoint and idempotent; distinct projections in each family are orthogonal and each family sums to the identity. By [F8], their lifted maps $P_a\otimes I_B$ and $I_A\otimes Q_b$ are self-adjoint idempotents, and each lifted family sums to $I_{A\otimes B}$.

The product basis $(e_a\otimes g_b)_{a,b}$ is orthonormal by [F4]. Therefore the coordinates of $\psi$ satisfy $\sum_{a,b}|c_{a,b}|^2=1$. By [F7], $\rho=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$ has matrix $v v^\dagger$, so for every coordinate vector $u$ its quadratic form is $u^\dagger v v^\dagger u=|v^\dagger u|^2\ge0$ and its trace is $\sum_{a,b}|c_{a,b}|^2=1$. Hence $\rho$ is a density operator by [F6].

Each branch map is complex-linear. For any finite reference register $R$, write an operator $Q$ on $(A\otimes B)\otimes R$ in the ancilla blocks of [F2]. Its amplified branch sends each block $Q_{ij}$ to $CQ_{ij}C$, so [F8] identifies the full block matrix as $Q'=(C\otimes I_R)Q(C\otimes I_R)$, where $C$ is the lifted projector from step 1.1. If $Q$ is nonnegative, then $Q'$ is self-adjoint and $\langle Q'u,u\rangle=\langle Q(C\otimes I_R)u,(C\otimes I_R)u\rangle\ge0$ for every $u$ by [F3], so every amplification preserves nonnegative operators. Thus each branch is completely positive by [F2].

Write $v$ for the coordinate column of $\psi$ and $C$ for either lifted projector. By [F7], the corresponding branch is $Cvv^\dagger C=(Cv)(Cv)^\dagger$. For outcome $a$, $(P_a\otimes I_B)\psi=\sum_b c_{a,b}e_a\otimes g_b$, so the diagonal entry at each coordinate $(a,b)$ is $|c_{a,b}|^2$ and every other diagonal entry is zero; off-diagonal entries within the selected $a$-subspace can be nonzero. Its trace is $\sum_b|c_{a,b}|^2$. For outcome $b$, $(I_A\otimes Q_b)\psi=\sum_a c_{a,b}e_a\otimes g_b$, so the diagonal entry at each coordinate $(a,b)$ is $|c_{a,b}|^2$ and every other diagonal entry is zero; off-diagonal entries within the selected $b$-subspace can be nonzero. Its trace is $\sum_a|c_{a,b}|^2$. These traces are the asserted probabilities by [F1].

For every operator $R$, cyclicity of trace and idempotence give $\sum_a\operatorname{tr}((P_a\otimes I_B)R(P_a\otimes I_B)) =\operatorname{tr}\!\left(R\sum_a(P_a\otimes I_B)\right) =\operatorname{tr}(R).$ The same calculation gives $\sum_b\operatorname{tr}((I_A\otimes Q_b)R(I_A\otimes Q_b))=\operatorname{tr}(R)$. Together with step 2.1 these are the finite-instrument conditions of [F1].

If a branch vector $w=C\psi$ has positive probability $p=\sum_i|w_i|^2$ from step 2.2, its conditional operator in [F1] is $|(w/\sqrt p)\rangle\langle(w/\sqrt p)|$. Its coordinate quadratic form is nonnegative and its trace is $\sum_i|w_i|^2/p=1$, so it is a density operator by [F6]–[F7]; a zero-probability branch has no conditional state by [F1].

Inputs are integers $n,m\ge0$, $n$ distinct ordered Boolean input wires, an $m$-bit target register $y$ disjoint from the input wires, and a finite Boolean DAG with an explicit topological order and an ordered list of exactly $m$ output ports. Every vertex has a unique identifier; each non-input node is a constant $0$ or $1$, a NOT node of fan-in one, or an AND or OR node of fan-in two. Each source reference must name an input vertex or an earlier node in the supplied order. Each output port may name any input or non-input node, and repeated output ports are allowed. The Boolean graph uses the NOT/AND/OR basis with constants from [[def-boolean-circuit-size-depth-fanin-and-basis]], extended here to multiple ordered output ports sharing one graph.

Return INVALID if the input wires or graph vertices do not have distinct identifiers, a target wire overlaps an input or graph vertex, an unsupported gate or incorrect fan-in occurs, a source reference is unavailable at that position, the supplied order is invalid, or an output port names no available vertex. Otherwise:

1. Allocate one fresh clean value bit $w_v$ for each non-input node $v$.
2. Process nodes in the supplied order. Leave a constant-$0$ bit untouched; apply $X$ to a constant-$1$ bit. For a NOT node with input wire $u$, apply $X(w_v)$ then $\operatorname{CNOT}_{u\to w_v}$. For an AND node with inputs $u,v$, apply $T(u,v,w_v)$. For an OR node, apply $\operatorname{CNOT}_{u\to w_v}$, then $\operatorname{CNOT}_{v\to w_v}$, then $T(u,v,w_v)$. If a two-port node uses the same source identifier twice, first allocate a fresh clean scratch bit $s$, copy the source into $s$ by CNOT, use the distinct physical wires as the gate inputs, and uncopy $s$ immediately after writing $w_v$.
3. For each output port $j$, apply CNOT from its named input or value wire to target bit $y_j$.
4. Append the inverse of the entire node-evaluation list in reverse chronological order, including the temporary source-copy and uncopy instructions. Return the resulting finite gate list, with the input register unchanged and the target changed only by the stated XOR into $y$.

The inverse-list operation is defined instruction by instruction: $X$, CNOT, and Toffoli are each replaced by themselves, in reverse order. The Boolean graph is an explicit finite input; this procedure makes no uniform-generation, oracle, or Turing-time claim.

Let $n,m\ge0$, $x\in\{0,1\}^n$, and $y\in\{0,1\}^m$. Let a finite topologically ordered Boolean DAG have $S$ non-input nodes, including constants, and $E$ input-port uses counted with multiplicity. Its gates are NOT, AND, OR, and constants, with fan-in at most two, and it has $m$ ordered output ports computing $f(x)$. Under the fixed elementary alphabet in [[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]], counting each occurrence of $X$, CNOT, and Toffoli as one gate and one serial layer, [[alg-qc-reversible-embedding]] returns a circuit on the ordered input, target, and work registers implementing
$$
|x,y,0^w\rangle\longmapsto|x,y\oplus f(x),0^w\rangle
$$
for every basis input $x$ and every target string $y$. It uses at most $6S+4E+m$ elementary gate occurrences, at most $S+E$ clean work bits, and serial depth at most $6S+4E+m$. The same operator action holds coherently on arbitrary superpositions and after adjoining any finite reference register.

Let $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The one-qubit generators and exact matrices in the
ordered computational basis are

$$H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega\end{pmatrix},\qquad T^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$

On basis vectors, $H|q\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^q|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and
$T^k|q\rangle=\omega^{kq}|q\rangle$ for $q\in\{0,1\}$.

Write $S=T^2=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)$ and
$Z=T^4=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. Pauli $X,Y,Z$ are as in
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]]. On two ordered wires,
$\operatorname{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,b\mathbin\oplus a\rangle$; the first wire
is control and the second target. A circuit is a finite chronological word of
these gates at stated wire positions; its matrix is the product with later
gates on the left. No extra wire or controlled-$T$ operation is implicit.

The scalar phase $\omega I$ is an allowed Clifford phase in the one-qubit
matrix-word convention. Its scalar factor is retained in exact matrix products;
the convention that an overall scalar does not affect a resource count is
stated separately from matrix equality. It does not grant a controlled-$T$
operation or allow a scalar on a target wire to be discarded under control.

The exact one-qubit H/T algebra is generated by $H,T,T^\dagger$; $S$ and $Z$
are aliases for the displayed powers. The distinction between exact matrix
equality and [[def-qc-global-phase-equivalence|global-phase equivalence]] is
maintained. Resource costs are supplied by
[[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]] and remain separate from this matrix
definition.

Write $\mathcal Q_n$ for the ordered tensor product of $n$ copies of the two-level register from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]], with $\mathcal Q_0=\mathbb C$. Fix a finite gate alphabet $G$. Each $g\in G$ has an arity $r(g)\ge1$ and a specified unitary $U_g:\mathcal Q_{r(g)}\to\mathcal Q_{r(g)}$. An operation model states which listed gates may be called and what access or cost is assigned to them; the matrix $U_g$ by itself is only the mathematical gate data.

For $n\ge0$, the circuit wire set is $[n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ in its displayed order and its state space is $\mathcal Q_n$. The computational basis word $x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1})$ is assigned slot $\operatorname{enc}_n(x)$ from [[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]], so wire $0$ is the most significant bit and the empty register has its single basis vector in slot $0$.

A gate occurrence on the $n$ wires is a pair $(g,(w_0,\ldots,w_{r(g)-1}))$ with distinct wire labels $w_j\in[n]$; the tuple order is the input and output factor order of the local gate. A layer is a finite ordered list of gate occurrences whose wire supports are pairwise disjoint. A unitary circuit is a finite chronological list $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ of such layers, with $L_1$ applied first and $L_d$ last; $d=0$ is the empty circuit. Its input, output, and terminally measured wires are specified as ordered lists without repetitions in $[n]$. This syntax specifies finite data only; the semantic action of gates on the full register is defined separately.

For a gate occurrence $g=(\gamma,w)$ in a circuit on $\mathcal Q_n$, let $\widetilde U_g$ be the global embedding from [[lem-qc-local-gate-wire-embedding]]. For a layer $L_t=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$, define
$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$
For a circuit with chronological layers $L_1,\ldots,L_d$, define
$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

A **full-list uniform quantum circuit family** is a sequence $(C_n)_{n\ge0}$ together with one fixed deterministic one-tape Turing machine $G$ and constants $c\ge1$ and $k\in\mathbb N$ such that, on input the unary word $1^n$, $G$ halts within $c(n+1)^k$ transitions and its final tape is a valid self-delimiting binary description of the entire circuit $C_n$. The machine output convention is that of [[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]] and [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], and running time is as in [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]].

The following fixed-order code makes the full circuit and its designated input/output wires effective. A unary natural $r\in\mathbb N$ is written $1^r0$, including the one-symbol code $0$ for $r=0$. A self-delimiting binary natural $r$ is written $1^{|\operatorname{bin}(r)|}0\operatorname{bin}(r)$, where $\operatorname{bin}(r)$ is its ordinary binary numeral with no leading zeros and $\operatorname{bin}(0)=0$. The header gives the input-wire count $n$ and total wire count $m$ in unary, followed by the gate count $g$ as a self-delimiting natural; validity requires $m\ge n$.

Each gate record consists of a two-bit label ($00,01,10,11$ for $H,T,T^\dagger,\mathrm{CNOT}$ respectively), followed by one self-delimiting wire index for $H,T,T^\dagger$ and two ordered self-delimiting indices for CNOT. Every index is less than $m$; CNOT indices are distinct, with the first the control and the second the target. The list contains exactly $g$ records. After the gate list, an output-count self-delimiting natural is followed by that many ordered, pairwise distinct wire indices, each less than $m$. Parsing rejects every other label, malformed or out-of-range index, repeated output index, truncated field, or trailing bit. This defines a total decoder by returning a fixed malformed-code symbol on any invalid word; effective binary encodings and total decoders are as in [[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]].

The gate labels and matrices are the fixed finite library $H,T,T^\dagger,\mathrm{CNOT}$ of [[def-qc-clifford-t-gate-library]], with entries in $\mathbb Q(\zeta_8)=\mathbb Q(i,\sqrt2)$; CNOT is control-first. The remaining $m-n$ wires are auxiliary wires; their initial states are determined when a family is used in a computation model. This family convention adopts full-list generation. It makes no equivalence claim with indexed-gate uniformity and, in particular, does not assert that an indexed-gate generator can be expanded to the full list in polynomial time.

derivations.claim: For $a,b,c\in\{0,1\}$ set $d=a+b+c-(a\oplus b)-(a\oplus c)-(b\oplus c)+(a\oplus b\oplus c)$, with ordinary integer addition and subtraction. If exactly $k$ of $a,b,c$ equal $1$, then $d=0$ for $k=0,1,2$ and $d=4$ for $k=3$. Thus $d=4abc$.

Use one clean scratch bit $r$. Apply $T$ to each of the three data bits. For each of the three pair parities, compute that XOR into $r$ with two CNOTs, apply $T^\dagger$ to $r$, and undo the same two CNOTs. A **promise problem** is a pair $(Y,N)$ of disjoint subsets of $\{0,1\}^*$. Its promise is $Y\cup N$. A deterministic solver must accept every word of $Y$ and reject every word of $N$, with either answer allowed elsewhere. The pair belongs to $\mathrm{PromiseP}$ if such a solver has a polynomial time bound on every input.

It belongs to $\mathrm{PromiseNP}$ if there are a polynomial $p$ and a deterministic polynomial-time predicate $V(x,w)$ such that every $x\in Y$ has some $w$ with $|w|\le p(|x|)$ and $V(x,w)=1$, whereas for every $x\in N$ every such $w$ has $V(x,w)=0$. The promise need not be decidable; either side or both sides may be empty. When $Y\cup N=\{0,1\}^*$, this is the ordinary language decision convention.

For every fixed deterministic Turing machine $M$ that halts in polynomial
time, there is a polynomial-size logspace-uniform Boolean circuit family
$(C_n)$ such that $C_n(x)=1$ exactly when $M$ accepts
$x\in\{0,1\}^n$.

Let $(C_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a polynomial-size Boolean circuit family generated in the indexed-gate, logspace sense of [[def-logspace-uniform-circuit-family]]. Assume a fixed polynomial $q$ bounds the number of non-input nodes of $C_n$ by $q(n)$. There is one deterministic polynomial-time machine which, on unary input $1^n$, writes a complete self-delimiting topological gate list for $C_n$, including its input count, all node records and its designated output. The resulting list describes the same circuit and therefore computes the same Boolean function.

Let a finite Boolean DAG in the basis of [[def-boolean-circuit-size-depth-fanin-and-basis]] have $n$ ordered input bits, $m$ ordered output ports, $S$ non-input nodes and $E$ input-port uses counted with multiplicity. There is a deterministic compiler which, from its explicit topological list, emits a valid QC14 circuit over exactly $H,T,T^\dagger,\mathrm{CNOT}$ with the first $n$ wires as data, $m$ zero-initialized target wires, at most $S+E$ clean value wires and one additional clean scratch wire. For every $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ and $y\in\{0,1\}^m$, its unitary satisfies

$$ |x,y,0^{S+E+1}\rangle\longmapsto |x,y\oplus f(x),0^{S+E+1}\rangle, $$

where $f(x)$ is the ordered Boolean output. It uses at most $27(6S+4E+m)$ QC14 gate occurrences, and the full self-delimiting circuit list is produced in time polynomial in the Boolean-DAG description length. The same action holds on superpositions by linearity.

A promise problem $\Pi=(Y,N)$ belongs to $\mathrm{EQP}$ in the QC14 model if there is a full-list uniform family $(C_n)_{n\ge0}$ and a polynomial-time total acceptance predicate $A_n$ as in [[def-qc-promise-computation-model]], [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]], and [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]], using the exact gate and cost conventions of [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]] and [[def-qc-clifford-t-gate-library]], such that

$$ p_{C_{|x|}}(x)=1\quad(x\in Y),\qquad p_{C_{|x|}}(x)=0\quad(x\in N). $$

No condition is imposed on $x\notin Y\cup N$ ([[def-promise-problem]]). The finite output law is normalized by [[thm-qc-output-acceptance-law-normalizes]].

In this page, $\mathrm{ZQP}$ denotes the following bounded-failure zero-error promise class. A promise problem $\Pi=(Y,N)$ belongs to $\mathrm{ZQP}$ if there are a full-list uniform QC14 family $(C_n)$, a polynomial-time total label decoder $D_n(x,z)\in\{\mathrm{YES},\mathrm{NO},?\}$, and the finite output law of [[def-qc-promise-computation-model]], [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]], and [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]], such that for every $x\in Y$ the probability of $\mathrm{YES}$ is at least $2/3$ and the probability of $\mathrm{NO}$ is zero, while for every $x\in N$ the probability of $\mathrm{NO}$ is at least $2/3$ and the probability of $\mathrm{YES}$ is zero. All output strings receive one of the three labels, so the remaining probability is the allowed failure label $?$; the output law is normalized by [[thm-qc-output-acceptance-law-normalizes]]. No promise condition is imposed off $Y\cup N$.

This explicit fixed-circuit, bounded-failure convention is sufficient for the containments proved on this page. No equivalence with an expected-time quantum zero-error model or with $\mathrm{BQP}\cap\mathrm{coBQP}$ is asserted.

A promise problem $\Pi=(Y,N)$ belongs to **BQP in the QC14 model** when there exist a full-list uniform family $(C_n)$ and a polynomial-time acceptance predicate $A_n$ as in [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]] and [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]] such that, for every $x\in Y$,
$$p_{C_{|x|}}(x)\ge\frac23,$$
and for every $x\in N$,
$$p_{C_{|x|}}(x)\le\frac13.$$
By [[thm-qc-output-acceptance-law-normalizes]], $p_{C_n}(x)$ is the probability of the specified acceptance event and lies in $[0,1]$. No condition is imposed for $x\notin Y\cup N$ ([[def-promise-problem]]). The gate alphabet is exactly $H,T,T^\dagger,\mathrm{CNOT}$; its matrix entries lie in $\mathbb Q(\zeta_8)=\mathbb Q(i,\sqrt2)$ as specified by [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]]. This definition does not assert a BQP-versus-classical separation, nor does it assert an unproved equivalence with another circuit-uniformity convention.

For every finite promise computation, every length $n$, and every classical input $x\in\{0,1\}^n$, the output weights $p_{C_n}(z\mid x)$ from [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]] are nonnegative and sum to one over $z\in\{0,1\}^{|O_n|}$. For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Fix $n\ge1$ and put $V_n=\{0,1\}^n$, with coordinatewise addition $\oplus$ over $\mathbb F_2$ and cardinality $N=2^n$. For $s,y\in V_n$, define the dot product $s\cdot y=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}s_jy_j\pmod 2$. A table code consists of a unary header $1^n0$ followed by the $n$-bit words $f(x)$ in lexicographic order of $x\in V_n$; this identifies function instances with binary strings as in [[def-promise-problem]], [[def-finite-field-and-its-order]], and [[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]].

The YES promise set $Y_n$ consists of table codes of injective maps $f:V_n\to V_n$. The NO promise set $N_n$ consists of codes for which there is a nonzero $s\in V_n$ such that, for every $x,y\in V_n$,

$$ f(x)=f(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=x\ \text{or}\ y=x\oplus s. $$

The sets are disjoint: every NO function has a collision between the distinct inputs $x$ and $x\oplus s$. Its mask is unique, since two different nonzero masks would give a third distinct input in the same fiber. Classical query access returns $f(x)$ at a chosen address. Quantum query access is the coherent XOR oracle $U_f|x,z\rangle=|x,z\oplus f(x)\rangle$ of [[def-qc-coherent-function-oracle]], which is unitary and involutive by [[thm-qc-reversible-xor-oracle-unitary]]. Each call is one query; query charges remain separate from ordinary gate costs by [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]]. In the query model the table is not supplied as gate data; the table code fixes the promised function only.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

In a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$, events $A\subseteq B\subseteq\Omega$ satisfy
$$0\le\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)\le1,$$
and
$$\mathbb P(\varnothing)=0,\qquad \mathbb P(\Omega)=1,\qquad \mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A),\qquad \mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A).$$

derivations.claim: Consider the finite input distribution that chooses YES or NO with probability $1/2$. In the YES case choose a uniform permutation of $V_n$. In the NO case choose a uniform nonzero mask $s$, then a uniform injection from the $N/2$ cosets $\{x,x\oplus s\}$ into the $N$ output labels. Every valid NO function has a unique mask, and each mask has the same number of such injections, so this is uniform over valid NO functions.

It suffices to bound every deterministic query strategy: any randomized strategy has finitely many possible histories and actions up to depth $T$, so its conditional action choices can be represented as a finite distribution over deterministic decision trees. Repeated queries can be removed by caching their earlier answer, so assume every queried address is fresh.

Fix a deterministic strategy and a query index $k\le T$. Since $N\ge16$, the premise $T\le\sqrt N/8$ implies $k\le N/2$. Suppose its first $k-1$ distinct query addresses $x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1}$ have produced distinct outputs. Under a NO mask, this transcript is possible exactly when $s\ne x_i\oplus x_j$ for every $i<j<k$. Thus at most $\binom{k-1}{2}$ of the $N-1$ nonzero masks are excluded. For every remaining mask, the queried addresses lie in distinct cosets; the number of injective assignments of output labels to the unqueried cosets is $\frac{(N-k+1)!}{(N/2)!},$ independent of the mask. Hence, conditioned on this transcript, the mask is uniform among at least $N-1-\binom{k-1}{2}$ candidates.

The next address $x_k$ is determined by the transcript. At most $k-1$ candidate masks, namely $x_k\oplus x_j$ for $j<k$, make its output collide with a previous output. Therefore $\Pr[\text{first collision at query }k\mid\text{no earlier collision}] \le \frac{k-1}{N-1-\binom{k-1}{2}}.$ If there is no collision, $x_k$ belongs to a new coset whose output label is uniform among the $N-k+1$ unused labels, exactly as the next output of a uniformly random permutation. Couple the two oracle transcripts to use the same unused label until a Simon collision occurs; the adaptive address choices then also agree up to that time.

For $T\le\sqrt N/8$ and $N\ge16$, each denominator in step 3.1 is at least $N-1-T^2/2>N/2$. Summing the conditional first-collision bounds gives $\Pr_{\mathrm{NO}}[\text{a collision by query }T] \le \sum_{k=2}^T\frac{2(k-1)}N =\frac{T(T-1)}N\le\frac1{64}<\frac13.$ This also bounds the probability that the coupled transcripts differ.

Let $D$ be the deterministic decision bit, with $1$ meaning YES. Under the coupling, its outputs in the two cases differ with probability at most $1/64$, so $\Pr_{\mathrm{YES}}[D=1]-\Pr_{\mathrm{NO}}[D=1]\le\frac1{64}.$ Its average success under the equal mixture is $\frac12\bigl(\Pr_{\mathrm{YES}}[D=1]+\Pr_{\mathrm{NO}}[D=0]\bigr) =\frac12\left(1+\Pr_{\mathrm{YES}}[D=1]-\Pr_{\mathrm{NO}}[D=1]\right) \le\frac{1+1/64}{2}<\frac23.$ By step 1.2 the same bound holds for every randomized algorithm. A worst-case error bound of $1/3$ would imply average success at least $2/3$, a contradiction. Therefore at least $\sqrt N/8$ queries are required for all sufficiently large $n$, which is $\Omega(2^{n/2})$.

derivations.claim: By the factorwise tensor rule [F5], $H^{\otimes n}|x\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_{y\in V_n}(-1)^{x\cdot y}|y\rangle$. In particular the first Hadamards prepare $N^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in V_n}|x,0^n\rangle$. After one query the state is $|\psi_f\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in V_n}|x,f(x)\rangle.$ For each function-register result $z$ in the image of $f$, [F4] gives probability $|f^{-1}(z)|/N$ and the conditional input superposition that is uniform on that fiber.

If $f$ is YES, every fiber is a singleton $\{x\}$. The conditional input state is $|x\rangle$, and the second Hadamards give amplitude $N^{-1/2}(-1)^{x\cdot y}$ at every $y\in V_n$. By the first-register instrument law [F4], its squared modulus is the conditional output probability $1/N$, independent of the measured function-register value; hence the unconditional sample is uniform on $V_n$.

If $f$ is NO with mask $s\ne0$, a positive-probability fiber has the form $\{x,x\oplus s\}$. Its conditional input state is $(|x\rangle+|x\oplus s\rangle)/\sqrt2$. After the second Hadamards the amplitude at $y$ is $\frac{(-1)^{x\cdot y}}{\sqrt{2N}}\bigl(1+(-1)^{s\cdot y}\bigr).$ It is zero when $s\cdot y=1$ and has squared modulus $2/N$ when $s\cdot y=0$. By [F4], these squared moduli are the conditional output probabilities. Pairing $y$ with $y\oplus e_j$ for a coordinate $j$ with $s_j=1$ shows that exactly $N/2$ strings lie in $s^\perp$. The conditional law is therefore uniform on $s^\perp$ and independent of the measured fiber label, so the unconditional law is the same.

In the NO case every sample lies in $s^\perp$, which is proper because $e_j\notin s^\perp$ when $s_j=1$. The span of the samples is proper, so its rank is less than $n$ and the algorithm rejects. The elimination procedure preserves row span under row swaps and row XORs; at termination its nonzero rows have distinct pivot columns and are linearly independent. They still span the original rows, so the pivot count is the matrix rank. At most $n$ pivots each inspect and update $O(n+2)$ rows of $n$ bits, giving $O(n^3)$ bit operations.

Each run reinitializes both registers and uses no earlier outcome as an input. Thus the conditional law of the next sample given any previous transcript is the same one-run law; induction on the number of runs gives the product law, and [F7] identifies the coordinates as independent. In the YES case each sample is uniform on $V_n$ by step 2.1. Their matrix has rank below $n$ exactly when some nonzero $t\in V_n$ satisfies $t\cdot y_j=0$ for every row $j$: Gaussian elimination uses invertible row operations and produces fewer than $n$ pivot columns, so a free variable can be set to $1$ and the pivot variables solved backwards to give a nonzero solution of the homogeneous system. Conversely, if such a $t$ exists, every row lies in its kernel; a coordinate vector $e_k$ with $t_k=1$ is outside that kernel, so the rows cannot span $V_n$.

Fix $t\ne0$ and choose $k$ with $t_k=1$. The involution $y\mapsto y\oplus e_k$ pairs vectors with opposite values of $t\cdot y$, so a uniform sample satisfies $t\cdot y=0$ with probability $1/2$. Independence gives probability $2^{-m}$ that all $m$ samples are orthogonal to $t$. Pointwise, the indicator of the union over the $N-1$ nonzero $t$ is at most the sum of their indicators; summing over the finite probability space yields $\Pr[\operatorname{rank}<n]\le (N-1)2^{-m}=(2^n-1)2^{-(n+2)}<\frac14.$ Each of the $m=n+2$ runs in [F2] makes one oracle call, applies two layers of $n$ ordinary Hadamard gates, and performs two finite register readouts. Thus the totals are $n+2$ queries, $2n(n+2)$ Hadamard gates, and $2(n+2)$ readouts; step 3.1 gives the classical elimination cost.

citations.quote: Let $N=2^n$ with $n\ge4$. A classical randomized adaptive algorithm that, given only classical query access $x\mapsto f(x)$ to the Simon decision promise of [[def-qa-32-simon-decision-oracle-promise]], must decide injective versus nonzero-mask two-to-one with worst-case error at most $1/3$ requires $\Omega(\sqrt N)=\Omega(2^{n/2})$ queries. Ordinary classical computation between queries is unrestricted.

For every $n\ge1$, the sample in [[alg-qa-32-simon-query-rank-test]] is uniform on $V_n$ when $f$ is YES, and uniform on $s^\perp=\{y:s\cdot y=0\}$ when $f$ is NO with mask $s\ne0$. The rank test rejects every NO instance. On YES its error probability is at most

$$ (2^n-1)2^{-(n+2)}<\frac14. $$

It uses exactly $n+2$ queries, $2n(n+2)$ ordinary Hadamard gates, $2(n+2)$ finite register readouts, and $O(n^3)$ classical bit operations.

Fix $n\ge1$ and put $V_n=\{0,1\}^n$, with coordinatewise addition $\oplus$ over $\mathbb F_2$ and cardinality $N=2^n$. For $s,y\in V_n$, define the dot product $s\cdot y=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}s_jy_j\pmod 2$. A table code consists of a unary header $1^n0$ followed by the $n$-bit words $f(x)$ in lexicographic order of $x\in V_n$; this identifies function instances with binary strings as in [[def-promise-problem]], [[def-finite-field-and-its-order]], and [[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]].

The YES promise set $Y_n$ consists of table codes of injective maps $f:V_n\to V_n$. The NO promise set $N_n$ consists of codes for which there is a nonzero $s\in V_n$ such that, for every $x,y\in V_n$,

$$ f(x)=f(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=x\ \text{or}\ y=x\oplus s. $$

The sets are disjoint: every NO function has a collision between the distinct inputs $x$ and $x\oplus s$. Its mask is unique, since two different nonzero masks would give a third distinct input in the same fiber. Classical query access returns $f(x)$ at a chosen address. Quantum query access is the coherent XOR oracle $U_f|x,z\rangle=|x,z\oplus f(x)\rangle$ of [[def-qc-coherent-function-oracle]], which is unitary and involutive by [[thm-qc-reversible-xor-oracle-unitary]]. Each call is one query; query charges remain separate from ordinary gate costs by [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]]. In the query model the table is not supplied as gate data; the table code fixes the promised function only.

Let $t,s:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$.

For nonnegative resource functions $a,b$, the notation $a(n)=O(b(n))$ means that some constants $c>0$ and $n_0$ satisfy $a(n)\leq c b(n)$ for every $n\geq n_0$. Every resource bound below uses constants fixed for the machine, uniformly over all its inputs and branches. Time counts transitions; space counts all cells visited on all tapes, including the input tape, with each distinct tape/cell pair counted once. No constructibility assumption on $t$ or $s$ is needed to define these classes.

A language $L\subseteq\Sigma^*$ belongs to **DTIME$(t(n))$** when there exists
a deterministic multitape Turing machine deciding $L$ in time $O(t(n))$.

A **nondeterministic $k$-tape Turing machine** is obtained from the deterministic
$k$-tape model of [[def-multitape-and-nondeterministic-machines]] by replacing
its transition function with a finite-valued transition map
$$\Delta_k:(Q\setminus\{q_{\mathrm{acc}},q_{\mathrm{rej}}\})\times\Gamma^k\longrightarrow\mathcal P_{\mathrm{fin}}(Q\times\Gamma^k\times\{L,R\}^k).$$
One branch chooses one instruction from the finite set at each step.

A language $L\subseteq\Sigma^*$ belongs to **NTIME$(t(n))$** when there exists
such a nondeterministic $k$-tape machine $N$ for which:

- every branch of $N$ on every input of length $n$ halts within $O(t(n))$
  steps, and
- some branch of $N$ accepts exactly on the words of $L$, in the same
  existential sense as [[def-nondeterministic-accepting-computation]].

A language $L\subseteq\Sigma^*$ belongs to **DSPACE$(s(n))$** when a
deterministic multitape decider uses worst-case space $O(s(n))$. It belongs to
**NSPACE$(s(n))$** when a nondeterministic multitape machine accepts exactly the
words in $L$, every branch halts, and the maximum number of visited cells over
all branches and inputs of length $n$ is $O(s(n))$.

Let $M$ be a deterministic $k$-tape Turing machine. For an input word $w$, let
$\operatorname{time}_M(w)$ be the number of steps in the computation of $M$ on
$w$ when that computation halts, and let $\operatorname{space}_M(w)$ be the
total number of tape cells that are ever visited during that computation across
all $k$ tapes.

If $M$ halts on every input of length $n$, its **worst-case time complexity**
and **worst-case space complexity** at that length are
$$ \operatorname{Time}_M(n):=\max\bigl(\{0\}\cup\{\operatorname{time}_M(w):|w|=n\}\bigr),\qquad \operatorname{Space}_M(n):=\max\bigl(\{0\}\cup\{\operatorname{space}_M(w):|w|=n\}\bigr). $$
Thus both values are $0$ when the input alphabet has no words of length $n$.

For a nondeterministic machine $N$, a **maximal branch** either is infinite,
ends in an accepting or rejecting state, or ends at a nonhalting configuration
with no allowed transition. Suppose that every maximal branch on $w$ ends in
an accepting or rejecting state. Since the computation tree is finitely
branching, it then has finitely many nodes: if it had arbitrarily large depth,
repeatedly taking the first child with descendants at arbitrarily large depths
would produce an infinite branch. Define $\operatorname{time}_N(w)$ and
$\operatorname{space}_N(w)$ as the maxima over these finitely many halting
branches. The worst-case values $\operatorname{Time}_N(n)$ and
$\operatorname{Space}_N(n)$ use the same input maxima with $0$ adjoined as
above, provided the branch condition holds for every input of length $n$.

We say that a machine **runs in time at most $t(n)$** when its worst-case time
is bounded by $t$, and **runs in space at most $s(n)$** when its worst-case
space is bounded by $s$.

Fix the finite circuit syntax and its complete self-delimiting binary description ([[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]], [[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]]). For a circuit $C$, let $L(C)$ be the number of bits in that complete description, $g(C)$ its number of gate occurrences, and $w(C)$ its total number of wires.

Each clean or dirty ancilla coordinate additionally requires a declared ordered partition of the circuit wires into data register $D$ and ancilla register $A$, and a declared target unitary $V$ on $D$. In that factor order, the complete circuit unitary must satisfy the corresponding exact contract of [[def-qc-clean-and-dirty-ancillas]]. For such a supplied clean contract set $a_{\rm clean}(C)=|A|$, and for such a supplied dirty contract set $a_{\rm dirty}(C)=|A|$; the notation suppresses the declared interface, which is part of the cost instance and may differ between the two coordinates. If no corresponding contract is supplied, mark that coordinate not applicable. These are counts of declared contract registers, not maxima over possible partitions. Zero initialization alone supplies neither return contract. Every auxiliary wire remains counted in $w(C)$ ([[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]]).

The gate sequence and supports determine a finite dependency order: each earlier gate occurrence must precede every later occurrence that acts on a shared wire. A **layering** assigns a positive integer layer to each gate occurrence, strictly increasing along those shared-wire precedence relations. Gates in one layer therefore have pairwise disjoint supports. Define the depth $d(C)$ to be the least number of layers in such a layering; if $C$ has no gates, set $d(C)=0$. If layers are written $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ in chronological order, the denotation is $U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}$, as in [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]].

For a family $(C_n)$ with a specified full-list generator $G$, let $t_G(n)$ be the worst-case number of Turing-machine transitions used by $G$ on unary input $1^n$. For a total acceptance predicate $A_n(x,z)$, let $t_A(n)$ and $s_A(n)$ be its worst-case deterministic transition count and tape-space use over all valid length-$n$ inputs and measured outputs, using a fixed effective encoding of the pair $(x,z)$. Any effective input description, classical preprocessing, or threshold computation has its own bit length and time/space bounds; these costs are not included in $t_G$ or $t_A$ unless the same machine performs them. The machine conventions are those of [[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]], [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], and [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]].

If the access model explicitly supplies a named oracle gate $\mathcal O$, let $q_{\mathcal O}(C)$ be the number of calls to it. With several named oracles, record a separate query coordinate for each. Ordinary finite-basis gates, oracle calls, circuit-description length, generator time, and classical bit costs remain separate; no oracle, controlled-oracle, inverse-oracle, or data-loading operation is assigned zero cost unless its interface explicitly says so.

For an approximate task with declared rational tolerance $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\ell(\epsilon)$ be the bit length of that exact binary-rational encoding. Exact finite-gate computations have no precision field. The **cost record** consists of all applicable coordinates
$$\bigl(L(C_n),g(C_n),d(C_n),w(C_n),a_{\rm clean}(C_n),a_{\rm dirty}(C_n),t_G(n),t_A(n),s_A(n),q_{\mathcal O}(C_n),\epsilon,\ell(\epsilon)\bigr).$$
An inapplicable coordinate is marked not applicable, not silently charged as zero. This definition records the resource model; separate theorems establish polynomial bounds.

derivations.claim: Let $N=2^n$ and $L=nN+n+1$, the length of the unary-header table code. For each of the $\binom N2$ distinct address pairs, scan the table to retrieve both $n$-bit outputs and answer NO if they coincide; answer YES if no pair collides. On a promised table this is correct, since YES functions are injective and every NO function has a collision.

One table scan and output comparison take $O(L)$ transitions, so the $\binom N2$ pairs take $O(N^2L)$ time. Since $N\le L$, this is $O(L^3)$; the explicit-table promise problem is therefore in deterministic polynomial time under [F4].

The oracle bounds in [F1] and [F2] charge calls to $f$ or $U_f$, whereas the explicit-input algorithm charges table scans and ordinary computation as required by [F5]. The deterministic $O(L^3)$ algorithm in step 2.1 contradicts the asserted absence of a polynomial-in-$L$ algorithm. Thus this oracle-query separation does not imply superpolynomial classical running time in the explicit-input length. This comparison does not refute an $\Omega(2^{n/2})$ time bound measured in $n$: the explicit table already has length $L=n2^n+n+1$.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

derivations.claim: The dot product with $s=01$ is the second coordinate, so $s^\perp=\{00,10\}$. Its span is itself and has rank one. Hence four NO samples cannot have rank two, and the algorithm rejects with probability one.

In $V_2$, the three one-dimensional subspaces are $\{00,10\}$, $\{00,01\}$, and $\{00,11\}$. Four vectors fail to span exactly when all four lie in one of these three subspaces. Each corresponding set of four-tuples has $2^4=16$ elements; every pairwise intersection and the triple intersection consist only of $(00,00,00,00)$. Inclusion-exclusion therefore gives $3\cdot16-3\cdot1+1=46$ failing tuples out of $4^4=256$.

By the independent runs in the given algorithm and the uniform YES law in [F1], each ordered four-tuple has weight $(1/4)^4=1/256$. Summing these weights by [F2], the exact failure probability is $46/256=23/128$. The union bound is $3\cdot16/256=3/16$, agreeing with [F1] and strictly below $1/4$. There are exactly four oracle runs by the algorithm's definition.
